transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Evelyn (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SRE), Priya (Orion Head ML Ops), Marcus (Platform), Anika (Security), Tom (SRE), Jules (DS)

Summary:
Quick, focused technical deep dive to diagnose high p99s Orion is seeing in production for streaming endpoints. Compare streaming vs batched/non-streaming behavior, isolate network hop effects (VPC peering + on-prem), and discuss KV cache hotkeys and quantization tradeoffs. Action: run controlled bench and share traces; Redwood to propose pilot config.

Topics:
- Observed symptoms (p95 good, p99 spikes)
- Streaming vs non-streaming token handoffs
- KV cache warm vs cold behavior and hotkeys
- Batching thresholds and head-of-line blocking
- Quantization effect on per-token latency and CPU vs GPU tradeoffs
- VPC/peering and network MTU/TCP settings impacting tail latency

Transcript body:
[00:00:12] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll try to keep this super practical — Evelyn will run through the bench and then we can drill into traces.
[00:00:22] Priya: thanks, Samir. we appreciate it. to set context, median token latency is fine, about 35 to 50ms, p95 around 120ms, but p99 spikes to 600-800ms intermittently which is killing SLAs.
[00:00:34] Marcus: yeah and it's mostly on our streaming endpoints; non-streaming batched endpoints look better, but we rely on streaming for real-time features so can't just switch.
[00:00:42] Evelyn: ok, good. quick clarifying q — are these spikes aligned with request size or with certain model variants?
[00:00:49] Tom: we thought it was longer contexts but we see spikes on tiny requests too. and we observed that during deploy windows there's a bump. could be cold starts, but dedicated service should avoid that.
[00:01:03] Diego: if i can jump in — network hops between our on-prem and the Redwood VPC could be adding variance. we saw TCP retransmits in a previous capture but haven't correlated to p99 yet.
[00:01:13] Samir: good, thanks. Evelyn, we'll start with an architecture recap then dive into KV cache and batching specifics.

[00:01:25] Evelyn: architecture note — for streaming we flush tokens as they're generated; that reduces first-token latency but can introduce many small writes across the network. non-streaming waits to assemble a chunk before returning which enables bigger payloads and more efficient batching on the server. so the tail behaviors diverge.
[00:01:48] Jules: does streaming increase risk of head-of-line blocking on shared GPU queues?
[00:01:52] Evelyn: yes, especially if you have a high-concurrency mix of short streaming requests and long context syncs. continuous batching can help but only if the runtime has a good batching policy — otherwise you get tiny micro-batches that overload scheduling.
[00:02:08] Priya: we do see sudden concurrency spikes during market opens which coincide with the worst p99s.

[00:02:20] [00:02:20] Evelyn: two quick hypotheses: 1) network jitter and small MTU or TLS renegotiation for streaming chunks; 2) KV cache cold misses or hotkey skew causing long tail to fetch weights or refill cache.
[00:02:33] Marcus: on KV hotkeys — we do have a few prompt templates that are used 40% of the time. could be hotkey.
[00:02:40] Tom: we instrumented cache hit rates and saw 88% overall but p99 requests often had cache miss streaks.

[00:02:52] Evelyn: ok, let's go through concrete diagnostics. first, networking: do you have VPC peering or direct VPN?
[00:02:57] Marcus: currently VPN with an AWS transit gateway; still traverses an on-prem firewall and a partner MPLS hop.
[00:03:07] Diego: that MPLS hop in particular can add variance if micro-bursts cause queueing. MTU mismatch could force fragmentation with lots of small streaming packets. also TLS session reuse matters — if client re-establishes sessions frequently you'll see spikes.

[00:03:25] Samir: right — we've seen MTU fragmentation cause odd p99s before, especially for streaming which sends many small frames. can you check your path MTU and packet sizes?
[00:03:33] Marcus: we'll pull pcaps. Tom, can you get an example capture from the window where you saw the 800ms p99?
[00:03:37] Tom: yep, i'll upload.

[00:03:40] [00:03:40] Evelyn: second, KV cache: how long is your session pinning? are you using prefix caching or full KV per request?
[00:03:47] Priya: we use per-user prefix caching for 12 hours in our app layer, Redwood is configured with a 30 minute kv cache TTL per your docs.
[00:03:55] Evelyn: ok that's fine in general. the issue is hotkey skew where a small set of prefixes evict each other causing refills. for example if 40% of requests target five keys, when those keys get evicted you'll see heavy synchronous refills hitting disk or network for model weights/kv refill path which shows up as large p99s.
[00:04:13] Jules: are refills synchronous? i thought the runtime does async refill.
[00:04:16] Evelyn: by default we try async, but if the refill path crosses network or disk boundary and your request needs that data to continue generation, it can block. plus if multiple requests trigger the same refill at the same time you get thundering herd.

[00:04:30] Marcus: any mitigations on the Redwood side?
[00:04:33] Evelyn: multiple — increase cache TTL for hot prefixes, use client-side sticky routing to dedicated pools, or enable adaptive prefetch for likely-to-be-used prefixes; also consider soft-sticky routing for users that have high fanout.

[00:04:46] Diego: question about batching: our traffic is bursty with many tiny requests. batching seems to increase median but reduce variance. is that a tradeoff?
[00:04:54] Evelyn: yes. batches amortize per-request overhead and reduce GPU kernel launch jitter; however, batching increases head-of-line blocking for streaming because you may delay small responses while waiting to fill the batch. for interactive streaming you want small max batch and aggressive partial flush policies. for background non-interactive you set larger batch window.

[00:05:12] Priya: can we quantify — what batch size or wait window is typical for 8xA100 class?
[00:05:18] Evelyn: general guidance: for real-time streaming on 8xA100, keep max batch under 8-16 requests and flush windows under 50ms when you want low first-token latency; for throughput-focused, batches of 64+ with 80-120ms windows get much better token/sec cost. but tune to request length distribution.

[00:05:33] [00:05:33] Samir: note these are starting points; we'll run an experiment with Orion traffic profile.

[00:05:40] Tom: curious — quantization was suggested internally to lower cost. does quantization change tail behavior?
[00:05:45] Evelyn: it can — int8 or int4 quantized kernels reduce compute and memory, which usually lowers median and p95, but tail can increase in some cases because quantized kernels sometimes fall back to slower code paths for specific ops or attention patterns, and those fallbacks appear at p99. also quantization can increase variance if the runtime picks different kernels dynamically.
[00:06:03] Jules: so quantization isn't a free win for stable tails.
[00:06:06] Evelyn: correct. we recommend testing quantized builds side-by-side with production traffic to confirm p99 behavior.

[00:06:15] Marcus: what about streaming protocol — are you recommending HTTP/2 or websockets?
[00:06:19] Samir: both are supported. websockets maintain a single persistent connection which helps with TLS reuse and is often lower variance for streaming; HTTP/2 is ok but some intermediaries terminate or reset streams which increases jitter. if you have firewalls or proxies that terminate long-lived connections, websockets may be better.

[00:06:36] Anika: security note — we must ensure TLS handshakes and SSO don't cause renegotiation. will persistent connections impact our cert rotation workflows?
[00:06:43] Samir: cert rotation needs planning but Redwood supports session resumption and automatic session key rollover; we can coordinate.

[00:06:51] [00:06:51] Evelyn: next let's look at a recent sample trace Tom uploaded.
[00:06:56] Tom: link: https://redwood.temp/upload/trace-orion-1119 — contains p95/p99 traces and packet capture.
[00:07:01] Evelyn: (scanning) ok i see a pattern — request arrives, small streaming frames, then a 420ms gap before the next token, and then continued streaming. gap correlates with a TCP retransmit and a fsync on refill path. that suggests both network and local refill happened together.
[00:07:18] Diego: fsync? which process is doing fsync?
[00:07:20] Evelyn: looks like a checkpoint or a disk-backed cache refill, could be model shards being pulled from shared storage into node-local nvme when cache miss occurs.
[00:07:28] Priya: we saw disk IO at the same time — our infra team confirmed a scheduled backup kicked off during one of those windows.
[00:07:34] Marcus: oh — so it's an infra scheduling collision.
[00:07:37] Samir: that can definitely spike p99. best practice: avoid heavy disk IO on serving nodes during market opens; use node pinning and separate storage for refills or warm caches ahead of time.

[00:07:48] Jules: what about retry policies? sometimes retries make tail worse.
[00:07:52] Evelyn: yes, retries can amplify spikes. prefer client-side hedging with jittered backoff or limit retries for latency-sensitive endpoints. Redwood supports hedged requests to alternate pools to reduce tail.

[00:08:02] [00:08:02] Samir: let's enumerate likely root causes: network jitter (MPLS hop, MTU, TLS session reuse), KV cache hotkey refills and thundering herd, disk IO scheduled jobs, batching misconfigs, and quantization kernel fallbacks.
[00:08:17] Tom: agreed. any quick fixes?
[00:08:19] Evelyn: short-term: 1) enforce affinity for hot prefixes to dedicated pools; 2) increase KV TTL temporarily; 3) disable background backups on serving nodes during peak; 4) switch streaming clients to websocket with session resumption; 5) tune batch flush window to 30-50ms.

[00:08:38] Marcus: longer term?
[00:08:40] Evelyn: longer term — move to peered VPC or direct connect to remove MPLS hop, add warmers for KV cache prefetching, and consider small dedicated pools for market-open traffic to isolate interference. Also run quantization A/B tests to confirm tail behavior.

[00:08:55] Diego: are there Redwood runtime knobs we should know about?
[00:08:58] Evelyn: yes — batch_max_size, batch_flush_ms, streaming_chunk_ms, kv_ttl_ms, prefetch_prob, and adaptive_batching=true/false. We'll include recommended values in the follow-up.

[00:09:10] Samir: i want to call out adaptive batching — for mixed workloads it's often better; it dynamically trades latency for throughput based on current queue depth. but it requires good tracing to tune.

[00:09:20] Priya: can we get a proposed config for our 3 use-cases: market open low-latency streaming, background analytics (high throughput), and mixed interactive?
[00:09:29] Samir: yes we'll provide three profiles. Evelyn will run the bench with your traces to validate.

[00:09:36] [00:09:36] Evelyn: about the bench — we'll replay real request arrival patterns including concurrency spikes, streaming vs non-streaming traffic mix, and we will report median/p95/p99 and token per second and cost estimates. we will also run with kv warm and kv cold scenarios.

[00:09:51] Tom: what about observability — what traces do you need?
[00:09:55] Evelyn: client-side request IDs for end-to-end correlation, server-side detailed spans for queueing, batch formation, kernel time, kv hit/miss, and network span for first-byte and retransmit events. packet capture for MTU/fragmentation if possible.

[00:10:06] Marcus: we'll collect a 2-hour window around market open and send three examples with high p99.

[00:10:12] Anika: security: we'll need the SOC2 docs and to confirm session resumption meets our threat model.
[00:10:17] Samir: will send SOC2 and TLS architecture doc.

[00:10:22] [00:10:22] Evelyn: one more nuance on streaming vs non-streaming: streaming can surface backpressure from the client; if the client reads slowly it can cause the server write buffer to fill and create blocking. double-check client-side read loop.
[00:10:36] Jules: i think our client is single-threaded and may block when UI updates. we'll review.

[00:10:43] Tom: do you have examples where switching to non-streaming actually lowered p99?
[00:10:47] Evelyn: yes — in another customer we saw p99 drop from ~700ms to 180ms by batching small streaming writes into chunked non-streaming responses during peak. but that came at a cost of first-token latency which they mitigated by smaller partial flushes.

[00:10:59] [00:10:59] Samir: ok, let's capture experimental plan: run bench w/ these variants — streaming websocket persistent sessions, streaming http2 with small frames, non-streaming batched, each with kv warm/cold and quantized vs fp16 builds. we'll compare p50/p95/p99 and token throughput.

[00:11:20] Marcus: timeline?
[00:11:22] Evelyn: we'll start the bench Monday, results by Thursday.

[00:11:27] Priya: great. any other operational tips?
[00:11:30] Diego: monitor socket queue lengths, GC pauses (if you run app layer in JVM), and nvme latency. those often correlate with spikes.

[00:11:39] Samir: also enable per-route tracing in Redwood Console so you can see token-level latencies and batch sizes.

[00:11:45] Anika: for pilot we'll need a limited dedicated pool, encryption at rest, and audit logs retention — is that supported?
[00:11:52] Samir: yes — Dedicated supports those and we can enable KMS integration. we'll include configuration notes.

[00:11:58] [00:11:58] Evelyn: quick note on kernel fallbacks from quantization — we'll capture logs for fallback events in the bench. if fallbacks are frequent you'll see p99 widening.

[00:12:07] Jules: any advice for preventing thundering herd on cache refill?
[00:12:10] Evelyn: staggered backoff on refills, prefetch warmers during low load, and jittered TTLs per key. also consider a small async prefetch thread pool to serialize refills rather than letting all request threads block.

[00:12:22] Tom: i'll add that to our runbook.

[00:12:26] [00:12:26] Samir: can we do a short recap of next steps?
[00:12:29] Priya: yes — orion to send traces and pcaps, redwood to run benches and share configs, security docs, schedule pilot discussion.
[00:12:38] Samir: perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the bench link and proposed pilot sizing.
[00:12:44] Marcus: thanks.
[00:12:46] Tom: thanks all. uploading traces now.
[00:12:49] [END]
